newsitem.title: USA: Jewell and Fox reach verbal agreement on movie.
newsitem.headline: Jewell and Fox reach verbal agreement on movie.

text.p: Richard Jewell has verbally agreed to give 20th Century Fox the right to make a feature film about his ordeal at the hands of the media and the FBI, one of his lawyers confirmed on Thursday.

Attorney Lin Wood declined to discuss the monetary value of the agreement but denied reports that Jewell had been negotiating for a deal worth about $500,000. But he said 20th Century's Fox 2000 had agreed to buy the rights to base a feature-length film on what happened to Jewell and his mother, Barbara Jewell, and their four-member legal team in the aftermath of last year's Olympic Park bombing in Atlanta.

Fox also acquired the rights to "American Nightmare: The Ballad of Richard Jewell," an article in the February issue of Vanity Fair magazine. But Wood, one of two civil attorneys retained by Jewell, said it could be 30 to 60 days before the Fox agreement is in writing and signed by all the parties.

Jewell, a 34-year-old former security guard, was first named by the Atlanta Journal as a suspect in the July 27, 1996, bombing that left two people dead and more than 100 injured at the Summer Olympics in Atlanta.

For the next three months Jewell was hounded by television news crews and federal agents, who searched his home but never found any evidence against him. The Justice Department publicly cleared him in October of all suspicion in the case and he has since embarked on a legal battle, suing various news organisations and individual FBI agents.

Fox 2000, a Hollywood studio owned by Rupert Murdoch's 20th Century Fox, cemented the agreement after overcoming stiff competition from Ted Turner's HBO and Sony Corp's TriStar Pictures, the Hollywood journal Daily Variety said.

Jewell has already reached settlements with NBC and Cable News Network. The deal with NBC was reported to be worth more than $500,000. He recently brought suit against Atlanta Constitution publisher Cox Enterprises.

CNN officials said on Thursday that Jewell also obtained an agreement that CNN's parent, Time Warner Inc, would discuss a possible book deal. The deal was not part of the settlement but during the negotiations CNN lawyers raised the possibility of exploratory talks with Time Warner, which owns Time-Life Books. Jewell and his mother Barbara assented to the idea.
Jewell's attorneys were quick to point out that the signed agreement in itself did not represent a book deal. CNN said neither side was obligated to anything.
